stimulus.text: The graph in the \(xy\)-plane shows the two lines of the system consisting of \(2x + y = 7\) and \(x + 2y = 8\).

stem: If \((x, y)\) is the solution to the given system of equations, what is the value of \(x + y\)?
rationale: Solve by elimination: multiply the second equation by 2 to align the \(x\)-coefficients, giving \(2x + 4y = 16\), then subtract the first equation: \((2x + 4y) - (2x + y) = 16 - 7\), so \(3y = 9\) and \(y = 3\). Back-substitute into \(2x + y = 7\): \(2x + 3 = 7\), so \(x = 2\). Cross-check by substitution: from the first equation \(y = 7 - 2x\), and substituting into the OTHER equation gives \(x + 2(7 - 2x) = 8\), so \(-3x = -6\) and \(x = 2\), \(y = 3\) — matching the marked intersection \((2, 3)\) on the graph. The question asks for the combination, so \(x + y = 2 + 3 = 5\). The live traps: a student who solves correctly but reports the first variable found grids 2 (or 3), committing the re-read-the-ask error — the graph makes this tempting because the dot's \(x\)-coordinate is read first. A student who multiplies \(x + 2y = 8\) by 2 on the left side only gets \(2x + 4y = 8\), and subtracting yields \(3y = 1\), a corrupted value far from 3. And a student who adds the original equations instead of subtracting gets \(3x + 3y = 15\), which happens to give \(x + y = 5\) only by coincidence here — on most systems that sign slip produces a wrong total, so the reliable method is the aligned subtraction shown above.
